To baptize someone means to perform a sacred ritual in which water is used on a person as a symbol of spiritual cleansing, a new beginning, and formal entry into a religious community — most commonly, Christianity.

The person performing the action (a priest, pastor, or minister) is said to baptize the other person. The person receiving it is said to be baptized.

The ritual involves water being applied to a person in one of three ways, depending on the tradition:

  • Immersion — the person is fully lowered into water and brought back up. This is practiced by Baptists and many evangelical churches.
  • Pouring (affusion) — water is poured over the person's head.
  • Sprinkling (aspersion) — a small amount of water is sprinkled onto the person's forehead. This is common in Catholic and Protestant churches.

No matter which method is used, the act is called baptizing.

Baptism is not just getting wet. The water is symbolic. When a person is baptized, it represents:

  • Washing away of sin — the water symbolizes the cleansing of past wrongdoing and spiritual impurity.
  • Death and rebirth — going under the water represents dying to one's old self; coming back up represents rising as a new person with a new life in God.
  • Public declaration — it is an outward, visible sign of an inward, invisible change of heart and belief.
  • Entry into the Church — it officially marks the person as a member of the Christian community.

In many Christian traditions, baptism is considered a sacrament — a holy act that God has ordained, not merely a human ceremony.

Infants: In Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, and many other traditions, babies are baptized shortly after birth. The parents and godparents make promises on the child's behalf. This is called infant baptism or paedobaptism.

Adults (or older children): In Baptist, Pentecostal, and many evangelical traditions, only a person who has consciously decided to follow Christ is baptized. This is called believer's baptism. Adults who were baptized as infants but later converted are often baptized again in these traditions.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

The verb follows natural English patterns:

  • The priest baptized the baby on Sunday. (active — someone performs the act)
  • She was baptized when she was three days old. (passive — very common)
  • He decided to get baptized after years of faith. (infinitive form)
  • They baptized him in the river. (specifying the place/method)
  • The minister baptized her in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. (the traditional formula spoken during the act)

Outside of religion, the word is sometimes used figuratively, most commonly in the phrase "baptism of fire" (or "baptized by fire"). This means facing an extremely difficult, stressful, or dangerous situation for the very first time — being thrown into the deep end with no preparation.

  • The young doctor's first night shift in the emergency room was a true baptism of fire.
  • He was baptized by fire on his first day at the new job.

The idea is borrowed from the religious sense: just as water baptism transforms a person, a brutal first experience can forge and define someone.

Less commonly, baptize can also mean to give a name to something — especially at a formal ceremony like a ship launch — though this use is rare and somewhat old-fashioned.

ConceptClarification
Baptize vs. ChristenThese words overlap. Christen often implies giving a name at a baptism ceremony, and is used more loosely (christening a ship). Baptize focuses on the water rite itself. In everyday speech, they are often used interchangeably for infants.
Re-baptismSome traditions do not accept a baptism performed in another church, so a convert may be baptized again. Others consider baptism permanent and irrepeatable — "once baptized, always baptized."
John the BaptistThe figure in the Bible known for baptizing people in the Jordan River — most famously, Jesus himself. His act of baptizing was an outward sign of repentance and preparation.

To baptize is to use the simple, universal element of water to mark a profound moment of transformation. Whether it's a tiny infant being held over a stone font, or an adult being submerged in a river, the act carries the same core statement: this person is being washed, renewed, and claimed — they belong to something greater than themselves.

That is why the word carries weight far beyond the physical act of applying water.
